 You Get Every Social Security COLA From Age 62 Whether or Not You’ve Claimed. The 3.6% Raise for 2027 Is Already in the Benefit of a 64-Year-Old Still Waiting, and Delaying Doesn’t Forfeit a Dollar of It
 By Vilma Rios 
 Published November 18, 2026, 4:03am ET · 4 min read 
 Tax Master desk. Editor: Vilma Rios .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Social Security applies every cost-of-living raise from the year you turn 62, so waiting to claim forfeits none of the 3.6% bump.
 A worker with a $2,000 benefit at 62 sees it grow to about $2,183 after three raises without filing a claim.
 Tax thresholds of $25,000 for singles and $32,000 for couples never adjust for inflation, so each raise pushes more benefits into taxable range.

 A traveler holds a passport and phone in an airport terminal, embodying the questions retirees face about benefits and Social Security. © Andrii Medvediuk / Shutterstock.com 
 Plenty of 64-year-olds hear about a cost-of-living raise and feel a sting. The money goes to people already collecting, and waiting for a bigger check at 67 or 70 can look like watching every raise go to someone else.
 The rules work in your favor here. Social Security applies every cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) starting with the year you turn 62, whether or not you’ve filed. The 3.6% COLA the Social Security Administration set for December 2026 benefits, payable in January 2027, goes into a waiting 64-year-old’s future benefit just as it goes into a 75-year-old’s check.
 Your Benefit Starts Collecting Raises at 62, Filed or Not
 Social Security first figures your primary insurance amount (PIA) at age 62. That’s the benefit you’d get at full retirement age. After that, each annual COLA raises the PIA itself. As one CFP’s widely shared guide of the benefit formula walks through, a worker who skips filing at 62 still gets the PIA rise by each year’s COLA, and the increases compound.
 The adjustment comes from section 215(i) of the Social Security Act. The tax code adopts the same procedure to index retirement-plan limits, 26 U.S.C. § 415(d)(1). Each COLA tracks CPI-W, an inflation index, from one third quarter to the next. This year the quarterly average rose from 317.265 to 328.746.
 Three Raises Already Banked by a 64-Year-Old Who Hasn’t Claimed
 Picture a example worker born in 1962. She turned 62 in 2024 with a PIA of $2,000 a month and hasn’t filed. Here’s what the COLAs have already done for her:
 COLA (effective December) 
 Rate 
 Her PIA afterward 
 Starting PIA at 62 
 None 
 $2,000.00 
 2024 
 2.5% 
 $2,050.00 
 2025 
 2.8% 
 $2,107.40 
 2026 (paid January 2027) 
 3.6% 
 $2,183.27 
 The new 3.6% raise adds about $76 a month to her future check. All three COLAs together add about $183, and she hasn’t collected a dime. Real figures will differ by a few cents because SSA rounds benefits down to the dime.
 Waiting Until 70 Multiplies the COLA-Boosted Number
 For anyone born in 1962, full retirement age is 67. Each year you wait past that earns delayed retirement credits of 8%, so claiming at 70 pays 124% of PIA. Those credits multiply the COLA-boosted PIA. At 70, she’d get about $2,707 a month, around $32,487 a year, and the COLAs from 2027 through 2031 would still be added on top.
 Waiting has a real cost: the checks you skip in the meantime, which matters for anyone in poor health. The COLAs, however, all stay with you.
 A Frozen Tax Threshold Catches More of Every Raise
 COLAs keep the benefit in step with inflation, but the tax test on that benefit stays fixed. Under 26 U.S.C. § 86 [ 1 ] , up to 50% of benefits can become taxable once provisional income crosses a base amount, and up to 85% once it crosses $34,000 for single filers or $44,000 for married couples filing jointly. Provisional income is half your benefits plus your other income, including tax-exempt interest. The base amount is $25,000 for single filers and $32,000 for married couples filing jointly. The law never adjusts those figures for inflation, so each COLA pushes more retirees over the line.
 Take her benefit at 70. As a single filer, she hits the $25,000 line with only about $8,756 of other income, such as an IRA withdrawal or a small pension. Past that point, each extra dollar she withdraws can also make part of her benefits taxable. Planners call this the tax torpedo .
 Medicare takes its share too. The standard Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90 [ 2 ] a month, and it’s deducted from your Social Security check once you’re collecting. Medicare’s income surcharge, IRMAA , uses your tax return from two years earlier. In 2026 the first surcharge tier starts above $109,000 [ 2 ] for single filers and $218,000 for joint filers.
 Smart Moves for the Gap Years Before You Claim
 Drop the COLA worry when you choose a claiming age. The raises hits you either way. Base the choice on your health, your cash needs and what your spouse would get as a survivor.
 Use the low-income years for Roth conversions . Before your benefits start, no Social Security counts toward provisional income, so converted dollars avoid the torpedo. From age 63 on, keep income below the IRMAA tiers, because those returns set your Medicare premiums at 65.
 Plan withdrawals around the fixed thresholds. Once benefits begin, every COLA uses up room under the $25,000 or $32,000 line. Taking larger IRA withdrawals before you claim can shrink the taxable slice later.
 When to claim and how much to convert are worth working out with a fiduciary advisor or CPA before you file.
